simple.headline: Think of it like sending a letter
paragraphs: The OSI model breaks down how computers talk to each other into 7 clear steps — like an assembly line. Each layer has one job, and it passes data down (or up) the line.
When you send data, it travels DOWN the layers on your computer, then UP the layers on the receiver's side. Each layer wraps the data with extra information (called encapsulation).
A simple memory trick: 'Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away' maps to Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application (bottom to top).

technical.headline: The Open Systems Interconnection Reference Model
paragraphs: The OSI model (ISO/IEC 7498-1) defines seven abstract layers that describe how network communications are structured. It is a conceptual framework used to understand interoperability between different systems and vendors.
Each layer communicates with the layer directly above and below it using service primitives. Peer layers on two communicating devices exchange Protocol Data Units (PDUs) using defined protocols.

layers.name: Application
layers.description: Provides network services directly to end-user applications. The layer closest to the user.

layers.name: Presentation
layers.description: Data translation, encryption/decryption, and compression. Ensures data is in a usable format.

layers.name: Session
layers.description: Manages sessions (connections) between applications. Handles establishment, maintenance, and termination.

layers.name: Transport
layers.description: End-to-end communication, segmentation, flow control, and error correction (TCP) or speed (UDP).

layers.name: Network
layers.description: Logical addressing (IP), routing across networks, and path determination.

layers.name: Data Link
layers.description: Physical (MAC) addressing, framing, and error detection (CRC). Divided into LLC and MAC sublayers.

layers.name: Physical
layers.description: Bit transmission over physical media — cables, fiber, radio waves. Defines voltage, timing, and connectors.

realWorld.headline: An HTTPS request — walking through all 7 layers
realWorld.scenario: You type https://google.com in your browser and press Enter. Here's what happens at each OSI layer:
steps: Layer 7 (Application): Your browser creates an HTTP GET request for google.com
Layer 6 (Presentation): TLS encrypts the HTTP request into a secured payload
Layer 5 (Session): TCP connection negotiation sets up the session between browser and server
Layer 4 (Transport): TCP segments the data and assigns destination port 443
Layer 3 (Network): IP adds source IP (your computer) and destination IP (Google's server)
Layer 2 (Data Link): Ethernet frames the packet with your MAC address and your router's MAC
Layer 1 (Physical): Your NIC converts the bits into electrical signals (or light/radio) and transmits them

commonMistakes.headline: Top exam traps about the OSI model

mistakes.correction: Layer 2 uses MAC addresses (physical, used within the same LAN segment). Layer 3 uses IP addresses (logical, routable across different networks). Switches use MAC (Layer 2); routers use IP (Layer 3).
mistakes.examTip: If a question involves sending data across different networks or the internet, think Layer 3 IP. If it's between devices on the same switch, think Layer 2 MAC.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking routers only work at Layer 3
mistakes.correction: Routers primarily make forwarding decisions at Layer 3, but modern routers also process Layers 4-7 for features like firewall rules (Layer 4), NAT, QoS, and deep packet inspection.
mistakes.examTip: On the exam, routers = Layer 3 device unless stated otherwise.

mistakes.mistake: Mixing up TCP and UDP layers
mistakes.correction: Both TCP and UDP operate at Layer 4 (Transport). TCP is connection-oriented with error correction. UDP is connectionless and faster but unreliable.
mistakes.examTip: If a question asks about reliability, retransmission, or three-way handshake — that's TCP (Layer 4). If it asks about speed or streaming — UDP.
